# Introduction

A retail company distributes product from three warehouses (A, B, and C)
to three sales regions. Management has three questions. Can the current 
inventory in the network cover projected regional demand? How is shipment 
volume actually distributed across warehouses and regions? And how
many additional truckloads should each warehouse send next week to enure there is
no shortage?

In this assignment I will answer the three questions using linear algebra rather 
than spreadsheet arithmetic. Part A treats inventory and demand as vectors and 
compares them per element to locate surplus and shortage. Part B represents shipment flows
as a matrix, where row sums describe outbound volume per warehouse and column
sums describe inbound volume per region. Part C expresses the restocking
problem as a system of three linear equations and attempts to solve it in
matrix form as $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$.

# Setup and Data Access

The three datasets live in a public GitHub repository I created and are read 
directly over HTTPS rather than from a local folder. Nothing needs to be downloaded.

# Part A: Inventory Analysis

## Building the Vectors

The inventory data forms a 3 X 3 matrix with warehouses on the rows and
regions on the columns. Each column is a vector holding the stock 
positioned for one region:

$$
\mathbf{I} =
\begin{bmatrix}
1200 & 900 & 800 \\
1000 & 1100 & 700 \\
900 & 700 & 1000
\end{bmatrix}
\qquad
\mathbf{d} =
\begin{bmatrix} 2800 \\ 2400 \\ 2500 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The demand vector is reindexed onto `REGIONS` rather than read in file order.
The two CSVs happen to list the regions consistently, but nothing is enforcing
that, and a mismatch would produce plausible-looking wrong answers instead of
an error.

```{python}
#| label: build-vectors
inventory_matrix = inventory_df[REGIONS].to_numpy()

# align demand to the region column order by label
demand_vector = demand_df.set_index("Region").loc[REGIONS, "Demand"].to_numpy()

print("Inventory matrix (rows = A, B, C | cols = Region1, 2, 3):")
print(inventory_matrix)
print("\nDemand vector:", demand_vector)
```

## Total Inventory Available in Each Region

Summing down each column collapses the warehouse dimension. This is the same
operation as taking the dot product of each column with a vector of ones,
computed below as a check:

$$
\mathbf{t} = \mathbf{I}^{\top}\mathbf{1}
$$

```{python}
#| label: total-inventory
total_inventory_by_region = inventory_matrix.sum(axis=0)

ones = np.ones(len(WAREHOUSES))
dot_check = inventory_matrix.T @ ones

for region, total in zip(REGIONS, total_inventory_by_region):
    print(f"{region}: {total:,} units")

print(f"\nDot-product check : {dot_check}")
print(f"Methods agree     : {np.allclose(total_inventory_by_region, dot_check)}")
print(f"Network total     : {total_inventory_by_region.sum():,} units")
```

## Surplus or Shortage Relative to Demand

We just need to subtract the vectors to get the buffer in each region. 
I calculated the coverage ratio by dividing stock by demand. Since the 
three regions are different sizes, a flat unit count is not comparable
across them.

$$
\mathbf{s} = \mathbf{t} - \mathbf{d}
\qquad
\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{t} \oslash \mathbf{d}
$$

```{python}
#| label: tbl-surplus
#| tbl-cap: "Inventory position by region"
surplus_vector = total_inventory_by_region - demand_vector
coverage_ratio = total_inventory_by_region / demand_vector

part_a_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Region": REGIONS,
    "Inventory": total_inventory_by_region,
    "Demand": demand_vector,
    "Surplus/Shortage": surplus_vector,
    "Coverage": coverage_ratio.round(4),
    "Status": ["Surplus" if s > 0 else "Shortage" if s < 0 else "Exactly Balanced"
               for s in surplus_vector],
})

Markdown(part_a_summary.to_markdown(index=False))
```

## Region Most at Risk

"Most at risk" is the region with the smallest coverage ratio. Ranking on
the raw difference alone cannot separate region 1 from region 2, since both
have the same buffer of exactly 300 units, and it also doesn't account for
the fact that 300 units is noth the same protection against 2800 units of 
demand or against 2400.

```{python}
#| label: risk-ranking
riskiest_idx = int(np.argmin(coverage_ratio))
riskiest_region = REGIONS[riskiest_idx]

print(f"Most at risk: {riskiest_region}")
print(f"  buffer   : {surplus_vector[riskiest_idx]:+,} units")
print(f"  coverage : {coverage_ratio[riskiest_idx]:.4f}")

print("\nRanked most to least at risk:")
for rank, i in enumerate(np.argsort(coverage_ratio), start=1):
    print(f"  {rank}. {REGIONS[i]:<8} coverage {coverage_ratio[i]:.4f}, "
          f"buffer {surplus_vector[i]:+,}")
```

The region carrying the least protection is **`{python} riskiest_region`** at
a coverage ratio of `{python} f"{coverage_ratio[riskiest_idx]:.2f}"`.

## Business Interpretation

Combining the 3 regions, the company holds 8300 units and has a demand of 7700,
so there is a cushion of 600 units. While the aggregate figure is helpful it 
can also be misleading since stock sitting in one region can't serve a customer
in another region. So, it's important to know if there is enough product but also
if the product is in the right place.

Regions 1 and 2 have a 300 units buffer, but those are not equivalent. Region 1
has a larger demand, so 300 represents a different percentage of stock in in region
1 and 2. Region 3 has no buffer, since the demand and stock are exactly the same. 
If some of the product is damaged or a shipment is slightly late, there will be stockout
as we can see in fig-inventory.

So, the network doesn't really need more units, it needs different distribution of 
the product among regions. If 200 or 300 units are moved from region 2 to region 3,
then all the regions will have a similar protection. Management should use coverage 
ration to define the safety stock policy instead of flat unit count because a fixed
protects a small region considerably better than a large one.

## Process Notes {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### What came up while building Part A

**Reading data from a URL is not the same as reading it from a path.** My
first working version pointed at a repository folder named `Assignment 1`. A
raw space is not legal in a URL, so I passed the path through
`urllib.parse.quote` to encode it as `%20`, and that worked. I then renamed the
folder to `Assignment1` and deleted the encoding step entirely. The workaround
was correct but it existed only to accommodate a naming choice I controlled,
and removing the cause was simpler than carrying the fix. The wider lesson is
that a path is just a string on disk, while a URL has a grammar, so file and
folder names that were fine locally become constraints the moment the data is
served over HTTP.

**The alignment issue I nearly shipped.** My first version read `demand.csv`
with `demand_df["Demand"].to_numpy()` and subtracted it from the column sums.
That works here only because both files happen to list the regions in the same
order. Nothing in the code enforces it. If `demand.csv` listed Region 3 first,
the subtraction would still run, return three plausible numbers, and be
silently wrong. 

**Where the math suggested the next step.** I started with the plain difference
$\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{d}$ and found it could not rank Region 1 against Region
2, since both showed +300. That dead end is what pushed me toward the coverage
ratio, and the ratio then exposed something the difference had hidden: the two
buffers are not equivalent, because they sit against different demand bases.
The limitation of the first operation is what motivated the second.
:::

# Part B: Shipment Matrix Analysis

## Constructing the Shipment Matrix

The shipment data forms a second $3 \times 3$ matrix on the same axes as the
inventory matrix: warehouses on the rows, regions on the columns. Entry
$s_{ij}$ is the number of units shipped from warehouse $i$ to region $j$.

$$
\mathbf{S} =
\begin{bmatrix}
300 & 400 & 500 \\
400 & 350 & 250 \\
500 & 300 & 200
\end{bmatrix}
$$

```{python}
#| label: build-shipment-matrix
shipment_matrix = shipments_df.set_index("Warehouse").loc[WAREHOUSES, REGIONS].to_numpy()

print("Shipment matrix S (rows = A, B, C | cols = Region1, 2, 3):")
print(shipment_matrix)
print("\nShape:", shipment_matrix.shape)
```

## Row Totals and Column Totals


$$
\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{S}\mathbf{1} \quad \text{(per warehouse)}
\qquad
\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{1}^{\top}\mathbf{S} \quad \text{(per region)}
$$

```{python}
#| label: row-col-totals
ones3 = np.ones(3)

row_totals = shipment_matrix @ ones3          
col_totals = ones3 @ shipment_matrix          

print("Row totals (outbound per warehouse):")
for w, t in zip(WAREHOUSES, row_totals):
    print(f"  Warehouse {w}: {t:,.0f} units")
print("  matches .sum(axis=1):", np.allclose(row_totals, shipment_matrix.sum(axis=1)))

print("\nColumn totals (inbound per region):")
for r, t in zip(REGIONS, col_totals):
    print(f"  {r}: {t:,.0f} units")
print("  matches .sum(axis=0):", np.allclose(col_totals, shipment_matrix.sum(axis=0)))

grand_total = shipment_matrix.sum()
print(f"\nGrand total            : {grand_total:,} units")
print(f"Row totals sum to      : {row_totals.sum():,.0f}")
print(f"Column totals sum to   : {col_totals.sum():,.0f}")
print(f"Marginals consistent   : "
      f"{np.isclose(row_totals.sum(), col_totals.sum() ) and np.isclose(row_totals.sum(), grand_total)}")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-shipment-margins
#| tbl-cap: "Shipment matrix with row and column totals"
margin_table = pd.DataFrame(shipment_matrix, index=WAREHOUSES, columns=REGIONS)
margin_table["Total Shipped"] = row_totals.astype(int)
margin_table.loc["Total Received"] = list(col_totals.astype(int)) + [int(grand_total)]

Markdown(margin_table.to_markdown())
```

## Which Warehouse Ships the Most, and Which Region Receives the Most

```{python}
#| label: identify-max
top_warehouse_idx = int(np.argmax(row_totals))
top_region_idx = int(np.argmax(col_totals))

print(f"Highest-volume warehouse : {WAREHOUSES[top_warehouse_idx]} "
      f"({row_totals[top_warehouse_idx]:,.0f} units, "
      f"{row_totals[top_warehouse_idx] / grand_total:.1%} of network volume)")
print(f"Highest-volume region    : {REGIONS[top_region_idx]} "
      f"({col_totals[top_region_idx]:,.0f} units, "
      f"{col_totals[top_region_idx] / grand_total:.1%} of network volume)")


for label, totals, names in [("warehouses", row_totals, WAREHOUSES),
                             ("regions", col_totals, REGIONS)]:
    tied = [n for n, t in zip(names, totals) if np.isclose(t, totals.max())]
    print(f"\nTies among {label} at the maximum: "
          f"{tied if len(tied) > 1 else 'none'}")

print("\nFull ranking, outbound by warehouse:")
for rank, i in enumerate(np.argsort(-row_totals), start=1):
    print(f"  {rank}. Warehouse {WAREHOUSES[i]}: {row_totals[i]:,.0f}")

print("\nFull ranking, inbound by region:")
for rank, i in enumerate(np.argsort(-col_totals), start=1):
    print(f"  {rank}. {REGIONS[i]:<8}: {col_totals[i]:,.0f}")
```

Warehouse **`{python} WAREHOUSES[top_warehouse_idx]`** ships the most, and
**`{python} REGIONS[top_region_idx]`** receives the most. Both totals happen to
equal 1,200 units, which is a coincidence of this dataset and not a
relationship since one is a row sum and the other a column sum, and they count
different things.

Warehouses B and C are tied at 1,000 units each. This is worth stating
explicitly because `np.argmax` returns only the first index at which the
maximum occurs and would silently hide a tie if one existed at the top.

## Business Interpretation

Warehouse A is the network's main concentration point, moving 1,200 units, or 37.5 
percent of total volume, against 1,000 units each from B and C. That concentration is a
single point of failure, meaning that a shutdown at A removes more than a third of 
shipping capacity, and the tie between B and C means there is no obvious second site
already running at scale to absorb it.

The more useful finding appears when Part B is read against Part A. Region 1
receives the most inbound volume at 1,200 units and also carries a comfortable
300-unit buffer. Region 3 receives the least at 950 units and is the one region
with zero buffer. The region under the most pressure is being served least
intensively. fig-shipments shows this in the right panel, where inbound volume
declines across exactly the regions whose coverage ratio is tightening.

Current shipping activity is not aligned with where the inventory risk actually sits,
and the fix does not require more total volume, only a reallocation of roughly 100 to
250 units of flow from Region 1 toward Region 3. The heatmap points to where that 
capacity already exists: warehouse A is Region 3's largest supplier at 500 units, while
C sends Region 3 only 200, so C is the lane with the most room to grow without
leaning further on the network's busiest site.


# Part C: Resource Allocation Model

Management wants to know how many additional truckloads each warehouse should
send next week. Let $x$, $y$, and $z$ be the truckloads shipped from warehouses
A, B, and C respectively, subject to the stated constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x + y + z &= 18 \\
2x + y \phantom{{}+ 2z} &= 26 \\
y + 2z &= 22
\end{aligned}
$$

## Expressing the System in Matrix Form


$$
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 1 & 1 \\
2 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 2
\end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{A}}
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{x}}
=
\underbrace{
\begin{bmatrix} 18 \\ 26 \\ 22 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{b}}
$$

The coefficient matrix $\mathbf{A}$ holds how each warehouse participates in
each constraint, the variable vector $\mathbf{x}$ holds the three unknown
truckload counts, and the constants vector $\mathbf{b}$ holds the
right-hand-side targets. Note the zero entries: warehouse C does not appear in
the capacity constraint at A, and warehouse A does not appear in the combined
B-and-C delivery requirement.

```{python}
#| label: build-system
A = np.array([
    [1, 1, 1],   # x +  y +  z = 18   total truckloads available
    [2, 1, 0],   # 2x +  y      = 26   capacity constraint at warehouse A
    [0, 1, 2],   #       y + 2z = 22   combined requirement for B and C
], dtype=float)

b = np.array([18, 26, 22], dtype=float)

print("Coefficient matrix A:")
print(A)
print("\nConstants vector b:", b)
```

## Solving the System Computationally

```{python}
#| label: attempt-solve
try:
    solution = np.linalg.solve(A, b)
    print("Unique solution found:", solution)
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as err:
    print(f"np.linalg.solve raised LinAlgError: {err}")
    print("\nThe system does not have a unique solution. Diagnosing below.")
```

`np.linalg.solve` requires a non-singular coefficient matrix. It did not
produce an answer, so the next step is to establish why rather than to reach
for a different function.

## Diagnosing the Coefficient Matrix

Three standard diagnostics identify the problem: the determinant, the rank of
$\mathbf{A}$, and the rank of the augmented matrix $[\mathbf{A} \mid
\mathbf{b}]$.

```{python}
#| label: diagnostics
det_A = np.linalg.det(A)
rank_A = np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)
augmented = np.column_stack([A, b])
rank_aug = np.linalg.matrix_rank(augmented)

print(f"det(A)                   = {det_A:.10f}")
print(f"rank(A)                  = {rank_A}")
print(f"rank([A | b])            = {rank_aug}")
print(f"number of unknowns       = {A.shape[1]}")
print(f"\nSingular values of A     = {np.linalg.svd(A, compute_uv=False).round(6)}")
```

The determinant is zero and the rank is 2 rather than 3, so $\mathbf{A}$ is
singular: its three rows are not linearly independent. The specific dependency
is visible by inspection once you look for it.

```{python}
#| label: row-dependency
print("Row 2 + Row 3 =", A[1] + A[2])
print("2 x Row 1     =", 2 * A[0])
print("Rows dependent:", np.allclose(A[1] + A[2], 2 * A[0]))

print("\nThe same combination applied to b:")
print(f"  b2 + b3 = {b[1] + b[2]:.0f}")
print(f"  2 x b1  = {2 * b[0]:.0f}")
print(f"  Consistent: {np.isclose(b[1] + b[2], 2 * b[0])}")
```

This is the decisive result. The second and third equations sum to exactly
twice the first on the left-hand side, so the third equation carries no
information the other two did not already contain. For the system to have any
solution at all, the constants must satisfy the identical relationship. They do
not: $26 + 22 = 48$, while $2 \times 18 = 36$.

By the Rouché--Capelli theorem, a system is consistent if and only if
$\operatorname{rank}(\mathbf{A}) = \operatorname{rank}([\mathbf{A} \mid
\mathbf{b}])$. Here the ranks are 2 and 3. **The system as given has no
solution.**

The same conclusion follows from elimination by hand. From the second equation,
$y = 26 - 2x$. Substituting into the third gives $z = (22 - y)/2 = x - 2$.
Substituting both into the first:

$$
x + (26 - 2x) + (x - 2) = 24
$$

The $x$ terms cancel entirely and the left side reduces to the constant 24,
while the first equation requires 18. The contradiction $24 = 18$ confirms that
no triple $(x, y, z)$ satisfies all three constraints simultaneously.

## Verification and Best Approximate Solution

Since no exact solution exists, verifying $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$
is not possible. What can be computed is the **least-squares** solution, the
vector that comes closest in the sense of minimising the residual
$\lVert \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b} \rVert_2$. Unlike
`np.linalg.solve`, `np.linalg.lstsq` tolerates a singular matrix.

```{python}
#| label: least-squares
x_ls, residuals, rank, singular_values = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)

print("Least-squares solution:")
for name, val in zip(["x (Warehouse A)", "y (Warehouse B)", "z (Warehouse C)"], x_ls):
    print(f"  {name}: {val:.4f}")

print(f"\nA @ x_ls          = {(A @ x_ls).round(4)}")
print(f"target b          = {b}")
print(f"residual (Ax - b) = {(A @ x_ls - b).round(4)}")
print(f"||Ax - b||        = {np.linalg.norm(A @ x_ls - b):.4f}")
print(f"\nExact solution exists: {np.allclose(A @ x_ls, b)}")
```

The residual is non-zero in every component, which is the numerical
confirmation that this is an approximation rather than a solution. The
least-squares vector misses the first constraint by 4 truckloads and overshoots
the other two by 2 each. It is the closest any vector can come.

## Locating the Error

Knowing the system is inconsistent is not the same as knowing which equation is
wrong. The rank analysis answers that too.

The dependency runs in a specific direction: the third equation's left-hand
side is exactly $2\mathbf{r}_1 - \mathbf{r}_2$. That means the third equation
contains no information independent of the first two --- and, critically, that
its constant is not free. Once the first two equations are fixed, the third
one's right-hand side is *forced*:

$$
2(x + y + z) - (2x + y) = y + 2z
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
2(18) - 26 = 10
$$

```{python}
#| label: locate-error
print("Is row 3 a combination of rows 1 and 2?")
print(f"  2*R1 - R2 = {2 * A[0] - A[1]}")
print(f"  R3        = {A[2]}")
print(f"  identical : {np.allclose(2 * A[0] - A[1], A[2])}")

implied_b3 = 2 * b[0] - b[1]
print(f"\nThe constant in equation 3 is therefore determined, not free:")
print(f"  implied by eq1 and eq2 : 2*{b[0]:.0f} - {b[1]:.0f} = {implied_b3:.0f}")
print(f"  stated in the problem  : {b[2]:.0f}")
print(f"  discrepancy            : {b[2] - implied_b3:.0f}")
```

**The error is in the third equation.** It should read $y + 2z = 10$, not
$y + 2z = 22$.

Strictly speaking, any one of the three constants could be the typo: setting
$b_1 = 24$ or $b_2 = 14$ would also restore consistency, since the requirement
is only that $b_3 = 2b_1 - b_2$. Equation three is the right place to locate the
error for two reasons. Mathematically, it is the dependent equation, so it is
the one whose constant is derived rather than independently given.
Operationally, correcting it preserves the stated fleet size of 18 truckloads,
whereas correcting the first equation would require inventing six truckloads of
capacity that management never claimed to have.

## The Corrected System Still has no unique solution

Fixing the constant removes the contradiction but not the rank deficiency.

```{python}
#| label: corrected-system
b_corrected = np.array([18, 26, 10], dtype=float)

print("Corrected system, b =", b_corrected)
print(f"  rank(A)     = {np.linalg.matrix_rank(A)}")
print(f"  rank([A|b]) = {np.linalg.matrix_rank(np.column_stack([A, b_corrected]))}")
print("  ranks now agree -> the system is consistent")

try:
    np.linalg.solve(A, b_corrected)
except np.linalg.LinAlgError as err:
    print(f"\nBut np.linalg.solve still raises: {err}")
    print("A is unchanged, so it is still singular. Consistency is a property")
    print("of b; invertibility is a property of A. Fixing one does not fix the other.")
```

With rank 2 and three unknowns, one degree of freedom survives. Rather than a
single answer there is a one-parameter family, obtained by treating $x$ as free
and back-substituting $y = 26 - 2x$ and $z = (10 - y)/2 = x - 8$.

$$
(x,\, y,\, z) = (t,\; 26 - 2t,\; t - 8), \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}
$$

```{python}
#| label: solution-family
print("General solution: (x, y, z) = (t, 26 - 2t, t - 8)\n")

feasible = []
for t in range(6, 15):
    candidate = np.array([t, 26 - 2 * t, t - 8], dtype=float)
    satisfies = np.allclose(A @ candidate, b_corrected)
    nonneg = bool((candidate >= 0).all())
    flag = "feasible" if nonneg else "negative truckloads"
    print(f"  t={t:>2}: (x,y,z) = {str(candidate.astype(int)):<14} "
          f"A@x = {(A @ candidate).astype(int)}  solves={satisfies}  {flag}")
    if nonneg and satisfies:
        feasible.append(candidate.astype(int))

print("\nTruckloads cannot be negative, which bounds the family:")
print("  z = t - 8   >= 0  ->  t >= 8")
print("  y = 26 - 2t >= 0  ->  t <= 13")
print(f"  feasible integer allocations: {len(feasible)} (t = 8 through 13)")
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-feasible
#| tbl-cap: "All feasible non-negative integer allocations under the corrected system"
feasible_df = pd.DataFrame(feasible, columns=["x (Whse A)", "y (Whse B)", "z (Whse C)"])
feasible_df.insert(0, "t", range(8, 8 + len(feasible)))
feasible_df["Total"] = feasible_df[["x (Whse A)", "y (Whse B)", "z (Whse C)"]].sum(axis=1)

Markdown(feasible_df.to_markdown(index=False))
```

Every row totals 18 truckloads, as the first constraint requires. The choice
among them is not a mathematical question, it is a management decision about
which warehouse to lean on.

## Business Interpretation

The constraints as written cannot all be satisfied, and no allocation of trucks
across A, B, and C meets them simultaneously. That is not a computational
failure but the substantive finding, and it comes with a specific address: the
third equation is wrong. Its left-hand side is fully determined by the first
two, so its constant is determined as well, and that forced value is 10 rather
than the stated 22. Management's combined delivery requirement for warehouses B
and C overstates by 12 truckloads what the fleet size and warehouse A's
capacity jointly permit.

Correcting that constant produces a workable plan but not a single one. The
coefficient matrix is rank 2, so one degree of freedom remains and the answer is
a family: warehouse A ships $t$ truckloads, b ships $26 - 2t$, and c ships
$t - 8$. Requiring non-negative loads bounds $t$ between 8 and 13, leaving the
six allocations in @tbl-feasible. Every one of them totals 18 truckloads and
satisfies all three constraints.

Which to choose is a management question, and Parts A and B are tied. Region 3 
has zero inventory buffer and receives the least shipment volume, and warehouse C
is currently its lightest supplier at 200 units. The allocations at the upper end of
the range give C the most truckloads, which is where the replenishment capacity for the
network's weakest region would come from. The lower end concentrates volume at
B, which does nothing for Region 3. The mathematics narrows eighteen truckloads
to six viable splits and the operational analysis picks among them.

So the answer to management is neither "here are your numbers" nor "this is
impossible." It is that one stated requirement is internally inconsistent with
the other two and needs correcting, and that even once corrected the
information given is insufficient to determine a unique allocation, which is
itself useful news as it means there is latitude to optimise for something the
original constraints never mentioned.

This is why systems of linear equations matter in logistics planning. A network
of any realistic size accumulates constraints from many sources and no one
reading them as a list can tell whether they are mutually achievable. Casting
them as $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ makes consistency a property that
can be tested rather than assumed, and it distinguishes three situations that
look alike on a spreadsheet: one workable plan, many workable plans, or none at
all. This scenario turned out to be the third masquerading as the first, and
then the second once repaired. Detecting that before trucks are dispatched is
worth more than computing a number quickly.

## Process Notes {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### What came up while building Part C

**I expected a number and got an exception.** `np.linalg.solve` raised
`LinAlgError: Singular matrix`, which I guess was the single most valuable moment in
this assignment. My first instinct was that I had built the matrix wrong, so I
printed $\mathbf{A}$ and checked it row by row against the three equations. It
was correct. The system itself has no solution.

**Knowing that a solution fails is not the same as knowing why.** Reaching for
`lstsq` to get some answer would have been the easy move and would have
produced three plausible-looking numbers with no indication anything was wrong.
Working through the determinant, then the rank, then the augmented rank, then
the explicit row dependency turned "it broke" into a specific diagnosis: rows 2
and 3 sum to twice row 1, so the constants have to as well, and $48 \neq 36$.

**The hand calculation and the computation agreed, which mattered.** Doing the
elimination on paper produced $24 = 18$, the same contradiction the rank test
found. I would not have trusted the numerical result on its own, because a zero
determinant is exactly the situation where floating-point arithmetic is least
convincing. Two independent routes to the same contradiction is what made me
confident enough to write it up as a finding rather than a mistake.
